# Unsupervised learning: clustering and mixture models {#sec-unsupervised}

The machine learning of the last three chapters was **supervised**: every observation in the experience carried the outcome, the recorded outcomes supervised the fit, and the performance measure compared predictions against outcomes the model had not seen. This chapter is about learning without an outcome. In **unsupervised learning** there is no outcome variable: the data are a set of observations on some features, and the task is to find structure among them, most commonly *groups* of observations that resemble each other. In Mitchell's definition from @sec-overfitting, the task and the experience survive: find groups, using these data. The performance measure does not, because there is no recorded outcome against which a proposed grouping can be scored. Chapters 6 and 7 relied on that measure, and the central question of this chapter is what to do without it.

Social and health scientists want hidden groups for several recurring reasons. Sometimes the variable of real interest was never measured, but other variables carry information about it: how students answer exam questions is indicative of whether they have mastered the material, and how a chat partner responds is indicative of whether they are human or a bot. Sometimes an effect is suspected to differ between kinds of people, without the kinds being directly observed. And sometimes there are simply too many variables to interpret, and the analyst wants to reduce them to a few interpretable groups, as marketing does when it builds "segments". The techniques of this chapter serve all three purposes, and they come in two families that the chapter treats in turn: **clustering algorithms**, which group observations by their distances to each other, and **mixture models**, which posit an explicit statistical model in which an unobserved, discrete variable produces the groups.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false" title="Before you start"}
This chapter relies on maximum likelihood and the likelihood-ratio test (@def-likelihood), the posterior distribution of @def-bayes, the definition of identification and the equivalence of models (@def-identification), the bias–variance tradeoff of @sec-overfitting, and cross-validation and the bootstrap from @sec-evaluation.
:::

## An example: Old Faithful

The Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone erupts every 35 to 120 minutes, and each eruption lasts between one and five minutes. The `faithful` dataset records 272 eruptions on two features: the duration of the eruption and the waiting time since the previous one. @fig-faithful plots them.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(faithful$eruptions, faithful$waiting,
     xlab = "eruption duration (min)", ylab = "waiting time (min)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Old Faithful: duration of 272 eruptions against the waiting time since the previous eruption. Two kinds of eruption suggest themselves: short ones after a short wait, and long ones after a long wait.](08-unsupervised-clustering-mixtures_files/figure-pdf/fig-faithful-1.png){#fig-faithful fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


Nobody labelled these eruptions, yet the picture shows two groups: short eruptions after short waits, and long eruptions after long waits. The eye performs unsupervised learning effortlessly in two dimensions. The methods of this chapter exist because real problems have ten or a thousand dimensions, where the eye fails, and because even in two dimensions the eye cannot say *how many* groups there are when the groups are less clearly separated than these.

## Clustering by distance

The algorithmic family starts from a simple idea: a cluster is a set of observations that are close together, so the raw material is the **distance** between every pair of observations. For continuous features the default is Euclidean distance, the ordinary straight-line distance in feature space, but the choice matters, and many other distances exist. Before any distance is computed, the features should usually be put on a comparable scale, typically by **standardization**: subtracting each feature's mean and dividing by its standard deviation. Otherwise a feature measured in centimetres contributes a hundred times more to the distance than the same information measured in metres, and the clustering becomes a clustering on whichever feature has the largest numbers. And beyond continuous features, distances have been defined for almost any kind of object: edit distance for text and DNA sequences, dynamic time warping and Fréchet distance for time series and curves, shortest-path distances for networks. Any method that accepts a distance matrix can therefore cluster any kind of object for which a distance can be defined, which is a large part of clustering's flexibility.

**Hierarchical clustering** uses the distance matrix directly. The agglomerative version starts with every observation as its own cluster, repeatedly merges the two most similar clusters, and stops when only one cluster remains; the analyst then chooses the number of clusters afterwards, by cutting the resulting tree at some height. How similar two *clusters* are, given the distances between their *members*, is a choice called the **linkage**: complete linkage uses the largest distance between members, single linkage the smallest, average linkage the mean. The linkage is a hyperparameter in the sense of @sec-overfitting, a setting the analyst chooses rather than a quantity estimated from the data, and different choices can produce quite different trees from the same data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
d_f  <- dist(scale(faithful))
hc_f <- hclust(d_f, method = "complete")
plot(hc_f, labels = FALSE, hang = -1, main = "", xlab = "", sub = "", ylab = "merge height")
abline(h = 4, lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Dendrogram of hierarchical clustering (complete linkage) on the standardized Old Faithful data. The height at which two branches join is the distance at which their clusters merged; cutting the tree at the dashed line yields two clusters.](08-unsupervised-clustering-mixtures_files/figure-pdf/fig-dendro-1.png){#fig-dendro fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


@fig-dendro shows the result for the standardized Old Faithful data as a **dendrogram**: a tree in which the height at which two branches join is the distance at which the corresponding clusters were merged. Long vertical stretches without merges indicate well-separated clusters, and cutting the tree at the dashed height produces the two clusters the scatterplot suggested. The dendrogram displays every number of clusters at once, from $n$ down to one, which is informative but also a reminder that the method itself never decides how many clusters there are. Because hierarchical clustering needs the full $n \times n$ distance matrix, it becomes expensive when $n$ is large.

**K-means** takes the opposite route: fix the number of clusters $K$ in advance, and search for the partition of the observations into $K$ clusters that minimizes the total squared Euclidean distance between each observation and the mean of its cluster, its **centroid**. The exact search is infeasible, since the number of possible partitions is astronomical, so the standard algorithm iterates two steps from a random starting assignment: assign each observation to its nearest centroid, then recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned observations, and repeat until nothing changes. Each step lowers the criterion, so the algorithm always converges, but only to a *local* minimum that depends on the random start. Two consequences follow for practice. The labels of the clusters are arbitrary, so cluster 1 in one run can be cluster 2 in the next, a phenomenon called **label switching** that also matters for the mixture models later in this chapter. And a single run can simply find a poor solution, so the algorithm should always be run from many random starts, keeping the best result; in R, `kmeans(x, centers = K, nstart = 25)`. @fig-kmeans shows the result for the geyser data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(8)
km <- kmeans(scale(faithful), centers = 2, nstart = 25)
plot(faithful$eruptions, faithful$waiting, pch = c(1, 16)[km$cluster],
     xlab = "eruption duration (min)", ylab = "waiting time (min)")
cent <- aggregate(faithful, list(km$cluster), mean)
points(cent$eruptions, cent$waiting, pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![K-means with K = 2 on the standardized Old Faithful data, mapped back to the original units. Crosses mark the cluster centroids.](08-unsupervised-clustering-mixtures_files/figure-pdf/fig-kmeans-1.png){#fig-kmeans fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 8.1"}
This exercise uses R. The `faithful` data ship with R, and `hc_f` is the tree fitted for @fig-dendro.

(a) Run `kmeans(scale(faithful), 3, nstart = 1)` ten times, calling `set.seed(s)` before each run with `s` from 1 to 10, and record `$tot.withinss`, the criterion K-means minimizes. How many distinct values do you see, and what do they show?
(b) Repeat with `nstart = 25`. What changes, and why?
(c) Cut the dendrogram of @fig-dendro at height 2.5 with `cutree(hc_f, h = 2.5)` and report the cluster sizes. Which of these clusters does the cut at height 4 merge?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.1"}
(a) Two distinct values: 56.1 in eight of the ten runs and 64.1 in the other two. Each run converges, but to a local minimum that depends on the random start, and one of the two minima is clearly worse than the other.
(b) Every run returns 56.1, the better of the two, because with 25 starts the best result is kept and a poor start no longer matters.
(c) Three clusters, of 125, 97 and 50 eruptions. The cut at height 4 merges the clusters of 125 and 50, which together are the long-eruption group; the cluster of 97 short eruptions is the same under both cuts.
:::

A useful way to understand what K-means produces is **vector quantization**, its application to images. Treat every pixel as an observation (its colour values as features), cluster the pixels into $K$ groups, and replace each pixel by its cluster centroid: the image now contains only $K$ distinct colours and can be stored in far less space. With $K = 100$ the compressed image is hard to distinguish from the original; with $K = 5$ it is visibly posterized; with $K = 1$ it is a single grey rectangle. There is no correct $K$ here, only a trade: more clusters reconstruct the data more faithfully, and more clusters take more space to store. Reconstruction error and model complexity pull against each other, as training fit and model complexity did in @sec-overfitting, and this trade returns when the number of clusters must be chosen in the model-based framework below.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 8.2"}
(a) A dataset records height in centimetres and monthly income in euros. What happens if these two features are given to `dist()` unstandardized, and why?
(b) A researcher wants to cluster daily activity curves from accelerometers, where the same activity pattern can be shifted in time between persons. Why is Euclidean distance between the raw curves a poor choice, and what kind of distance addresses this?
(c) In @fig-dendro, what would cutting the tree at height 2.5 instead of 4 have produced, and which of the two cuts is "correct"?
(d) A colleague reports "the K-means clustering" of a dataset, run once with `nstart = 1`. Name two distinct reasons the reported clusters might not be reproducible.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.2"}
(a) Income has a standard deviation in the hundreds or thousands, height in the tens, so squared income differences dominate the sum: the "clustering" is effectively a clustering on income alone. Standardization gives the features equal weight.
(b) Euclidean distance compares the curves minute by minute, so two persons doing identical things an hour apart appear maximally different. Elastic distances such as dynamic time warping align the curves before comparing them.
(c) A lower cut crosses more branches, so it produces more, smaller clusters: three of 125, 97 and 50 eruptions, as Exercise 8.1(c) found, instead of two. Neither cut is correct in any absolute sense: the tree represents the data, and the number of clusters is a choice the analyst brings to it, ideally on the grounds discussed at the end of this chapter.
(d) The random start can land the algorithm in different local minima with genuinely different partitions, and even when the partition is identical the arbitrary labels can switch, so cluster "1" need not be the same group across runs.
:::

## Model first or algorithm first

K-means is a different kind of object from everything in chapters 1 to 4, and the difference illustrates a cultural divide as sharp as the one @sec-explanation-prediction described. In classical statistical modelling the analyst starts from a *model*: a probabilistic description of how the data could have arisen, with parameters that are interesting *if the model holds*. Once the model is written down, how to estimate its parameters usually follows from standard statistical theory, typically by maximizing a likelihood (@def-likelihood); the computation follows from the model and is not itself the contribution. Machine learning often works in the opposite direction. It starts from a *computation* that produces something apparently useful; K-means is an example, an intuitive procedure with no probability model. The questions come afterwards: what is this computation good for, and how should it be evaluated, given the task? That order of operations, compute first and justify by usefulness, was proposed as a legitimate mode of data analysis as early as Tukey's "The future of data analysis" [@tukey1962], decades before machine learning made it routine. Neither direction is superior. Starting from a model gives interpretable parameters and principled inference, but requires assumptions. Starting from an algorithm gives flexibility and speed, but leaves unclear what the output represents. The next section takes the model-first route to the same clustering problem. Once a model is written down, the assumptions that K-means makes without stating them can be stated.

## Clustering with a model: mixtures

Suppose the height of every person on the planet were measured and plotted.^[The measurement is invented, but the rest of the section is real.] The left panel of @fig-height shows the distribution: clearly not normal, with two peaks that look like they might come from two groups. An obvious guess is that the groups are women and men. Had each person's sex been recorded, the guess could be confirmed by drawing the histogram separately per group, as in the right panel: within each sex, height is close to normally distributed, and only the combination is not. But suppose sex was not recorded. This happens constantly in research: the usability test that omitted handedness, the survey that could not ask the sensitive question, the attitude that cannot be measured directly at all. The groups are suspected but unobserved, or *latent*, and recovering them from the observed data is the unsupervised task.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- seq(1.40, 2.00, length.out = 400)
f_w <- dnorm(x, 1.62, 0.065); f_m <- dnorm(x, 1.77, 0.070)
mix <- 0.5 * f_w + 0.5 * f_m
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1.5, 1))
plot(x, mix, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "height (m)", ylab = "density",
     main = "observed")
plot(x, 0.5 * f_w, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "height (m)", ylab = "density",
     main = "the two groups", ylim = c(0, max(mix) * 1.05))
lines(x, 0.5 * f_m, lwd = 2)
lines(x, mix, lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![An invented population of heights. Left: the observed distribution, which is not normal. Right: the two groups that produced it, women and men, each normally distributed, with their sum as the dashed line.](08-unsupervised-clustering-mixtures_files/figure-pdf/fig-height-1.png){#fig-height fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


One idea that does *not* work is to split the sample on a guess about each person's sex and compute histograms within the guessed groups: without extra information the guesses will be wrong often enough to distort both histograms. What does work is a **mixture model**. Write the density of height, the height of the distribution's curve at each value, as a weighted sum of two normal densities,

$$
p(\text{height}) = \pi_1^X\, \text{Normal}(\mu_1, \sigma_1) + (1 - \pi_1^X)\, \text{Normal}(\mu_2, \sigma_2),
$$ {#eq-mixture}

where $\pi_1^X$ is the probability that the latent group variable $X$ takes its first value, and $\mu_k, \sigma_k$ are the mean and standard deviation of height within group $k$. (The superscript $X$ is not a power; it labels the variable the probability belongs to, a notation that is standard in this literature and becomes convenient with categorical data below. The groups are numbered rather than named because the model cannot know which component is "men": component 1 could equally correspond to women, the mixture-model version of label switching.) For one person the likelihood (@def-likelihood) is $p(\text{height}_i)$ from @eq-mixture; for the sample it is the product over persons, and its logarithm $\ell$ is what the estimation algorithm below maximizes and what the information criteria of @sec-mixture-fit start from. Fitting @eq-mixture to the observed heights recovers estimates of all five parameters, and with them the right panel of @fig-height, *without sex ever having been observed*. As the sample grows, the estimates converge on the true within-group distributions.

The result depends on an assumption. The model *assumes* that height is normally distributed within each group, and this assumption is not verifiable from the observed data, because the observed data are the mixture in which the groups are hidden. The assumption is what converts an impossible problem, unscrambling two unlabelled distributions, into a solvable one. Everything the mixture model delivers is conditional on it, a point this chapter returns to at length.

Estimation uses the **EM algorithm**, whose central quantity is also the model's main practical output. Start from a guess of the parameters. Given the guess, compute for each person the **posterior probability** of belonging to each group. This is the posterior of @def-bayes, for a discrete unknown: there the unknown was a parameter, here it is a person's group. Bayes' rule says that the probability of an unobserved state given the data is the prior probability of the state, times the probability of the data given the state, divided by the total probability of the data over all states. Here the prior is the class proportion and the probability of the data given the state is the component density, so the probability that a person of height $h$ is in group 1 is group 1's share of the total density at $h$,

$$
\Pr(X = 1 \mid h) = \frac{\Pr(X = 1)\, p(h \mid X = 1)}{p(h)} = \frac{\pi_1^X\, \text{Normal}(h; \mu_1, \sigma_1)}{p(h)} .
$$ {#eq-bayes-mixture}

Then update the parameter estimates using every person, weighted by these posteriors: a person who is probably a man contributes mostly to the male mean, but also a little to the female mean, in proportion to the uncertainty. Iterating the two steps until nothing changes maximizes the likelihood. The posterior probabilities are the model's answer to "who is in which group": not a hard assignment but a probability per person, acknowledging that group membership is genuinely uncertain. A small computation makes this concrete:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p_m <- 0.5 * dnorm(1.72, 1.77, 0.070)   # component density: men, at 1.72 m
p_w <- 0.5 * dnorm(1.72, 1.62, 0.065)   # component density: women, at 1.72 m
round(p_m / (p_m + p_w), 2)             # posterior probability of being a man
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.7
```


:::
:::


A person of 1.72 metres is more likely a man than a woman, but far from certainly, and the posterior of 0.70 says how much more likely. Where the two component curves cross, the posterior is 0.50 and the observation contributes equally to both groups.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 8.3"}
Use the parameters of @fig-height: means 1.62 and 1.77 m, standard deviations 0.065 and 0.070 m, and equal proportions.

(a) Compute the posterior probability of being a man for heights of 1.60, 1.695 and 1.80 m.
(b) Where exactly is the posterior 0.5, and why is it not at the midpoint of the two means?
(c) Recompute the posterior at 1.72 m if men are 30 percent of the population. What does the change say about the role of the class proportions?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.3"}
(a) 0.05, 0.50 and 0.98: the code of the chunk above with `1.72` replaced by each height.
(b) At 1.694 m, found by solving $\Pr(X = 1 \mid h) = 0.5$ numerically, for instance with `uniroot()`. The midpoint of the means is 1.695 m, and the small difference comes from the unequal standard deviations, 0.070 for men against 0.065 for women; with equal standard deviations and equal proportions the crossing is exactly at the midpoint.
(c) 0.50 instead of 0.70. The proportions are the prior in @eq-bayes-mixture, and a rarer class needs more evidence from the data before a person is assigned to it.
:::

### Latent profile analysis: mixtures of several continuous variables

With one observed variable the model depended heavily on the assumption. With several variables the model becomes both more useful and more credible, because the variables corroborate each other. The multivariate version of @eq-mixture, a mixture of multivariate normal distributions, is called a **Gaussian mixture model** in machine learning and **latent profile analysis (LPA)** in the social sciences. The two names refer to the same family of models, though not always to the same member of it: LPA as practised in the social sciences usually assumes that the variables are independent within a class, a restriction the Gaussian mixture models below need not make. Each component $k$ now has a mean *vector* and a **covariance matrix**, the table that collects the $q$ variances of the features and the $q(q-1)/2$ covariances (@sec-theory-to-glm) between every pair of them. In two dimensions those three numbers draw an ellipse, so a component is an ellipse: its centre is the mean vector, its size, shape, and orientation are the covariance matrix.

The covariance matrices can be constrained, and the constraints matter. Requiring all components to share one covariance matrix gives clusters of equal size and shape; letting every component have its own gives full flexibility at the price of many more parameters, since a covariance matrix in $q$ dimensions has $q(q+1)/2$ of them; requiring the within-class covariances to be zero, as LPA usually does, leaves only the $q$ variances. This is the bias-variance trade-off of @eq-bias-variance again: a rigid parameterization can miss the clusters' true shapes, a flexible one can chase noise. The `mclust` package [@scrucca2016] organizes these options in a three-letter code for volume, shape, and orientation, each either **E**qual across components, **V**ariable, or **I** (spherical): "EII" is equal-volume spheres, "EEE" is shared ellipses, "VVV" is every-component-for-itself. By default `Mclust` fits every parameterization for a range of component counts and reports the best model, chosen by a criterion that @sec-mixture-fit examines closely:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(mclust)
mc <- Mclust(faithful, verbose = FALSE)
summary(mc)
```

```

----------------------------------------------------

components:

      -1126.326 272 11 -2314.316 -2357.824

Clustering table:

```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Left: BIC for the mclust parameterizations on the Old Faithful data, by number of components; higher is better in mclust's sign convention. Right: the selected model's classification, with the component ellipses drawn.](08-unsupervised-clustering-mixtures_files/figure-pdf/fig-mclust-1.png){#fig-mclust}
:::
:::


@fig-mclust shows the criterion behind that choice and the fitted components. First, K-means is a special case of this model: constraining the components to equal-sized spheres (EII), the class proportions to be equal, and the posterior probabilities to hard 0/1 assignments makes model-based clustering computationally equivalent to K-means. The algorithm of the previous section is therefore a mixture model with assumptions that were never stated because no model was written down. Spelled out, they are strong: spherical clusters of equal size, which @fig-faithful's elongated clusters visibly violate. Second, the selected solution has *three* components where the eye sees two clusters. The reason is that the upper-right cluster is not elliptical, so the model uses two overlapping ellipses to describe its shape, and the mixture describes the *density* correctly at the cost of the component–cluster correspondence. When the groups themselves are the quantity of interest, two repairs exist: select the number of components by a criterion that rewards well-separated components (the ICL of @sec-mixture-fit), or fit the well-fitting mixture first and then **merge** components that overlap heavily into single clusters [@baudry2010], as `mclust::clustCombi()` does, which reduces these three components to the two clusters the picture shows; @sec-merging returns to this. The chapter maintains the distinction between *components*, the normal densities the model uses, and *clusters*, the groups the researcher means.

### Latent class analysis: mixtures of categorical variables

When the observed variables are categorical, the within-class normal distributions are replaced by within-class category probabilities, and the model is called **latent class analysis (LCA)**. It is the discrete-observed, discrete-latent cell of @tbl-lvm, which organizes the family of latent variable models by the type of the observed and the latent variables. Only the right-hand column is treated in this book; factor analysis and item response theory are not (the ACE model of @sec-theory-to-glm was a first example of the left-hand column, and Beaujean's book in the preface's further reading is the entry point to the rest).

|                        | Latent variable continuous | Latent variable discrete |
|------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Observed continuous** | factor analysis           | latent profile analysis  |
| **Observed discrete**   | item response theory      | latent class analysis    |

: Names of latent variable models, by the type of the observed and latent variables. {#tbl-lvm}

For three categorical observed variables $A$, $B$, $C$, the latent class model says

$$
\pi_{abc}^{ABC} \;=\; \sum_{x} \pi_x^X \, \pi_a^{A \mid X} \, \pi_b^{B \mid X} \, \pi_c^{C \mid X} ,
$$ {#eq-lca}

read as: the probability of observing the response pattern $(a, b, c)$ is a weighted sum over the latent classes $x$ of the probability of that pattern within each class, weighted by the class sizes $\pi_x^X$. The key assumption is in the product $\pi_a^{A \mid X} \pi_b^{B \mid X} \pi_c^{C \mid X}$: *within* a class, the observed variables are independent. This assumption, **local independence**, is LCA's version of the within-class normality assumption above, and it carries the same double role: it is what identifies the model, and it is what the observed data cannot fully check. It is also the mixture version of the assumption in @sec-theory-to-glm that every disturbance covariance not drawn in the diagram is zero: once the latent class is in the model, what remains of each indicator is specific to that indicator, so the class is the only common cause of the indicators. It also supplies the model's interpretation. The classes are constructed so that they explain the associations among the observed variables: people are similar within classes and different between them, and whatever relationships the variables show in the whole sample should vanish once class membership is held constant.

The LISS panel of @sec-theory-to-glm provides a natural application. LISS is run by Centerdata and is part of ODISSEI, the Dutch national research infrastructure for the social sciences (<https://odissei-data.nl>), which also organized the PreFer challenge of @sec-explanation-prediction and gives researchers access to the registers of Statistics Netherlands. The health module asks every adult respondent whether a physician has ever diagnosed each of a list of conditions. Ten of these diagnoses, from angina to cancer, are binary indicators of a respondent's pattern of chronic disease, and a standing question in health research is whether such conditions cluster into recognizable **multimorbidity** patterns: combinations that co-occur in the same people, such as the cardiometabolic cluster of hypertension, high cholesterol, and diabetes. The script `analysis/liss/06-prepare-lca.R` builds the dataset: 4,647 respondents with complete diagnosis batteries. The model is fitted with the `poLCA` package [@linzer2011].^[The LISS microdata cannot be redistributed, so this chunk cannot be run from the repository as it stands. A synthetic stand-in with the same variables, simulated from the models fitted to the real data, is shipped as `data-synthetic/liss_lca_conditions_synthetic.csv` (see `data-synthetic/README.md`); replace the `readRDS(...)` line by `read.csv("data-synthetic/liss_lca_conditions_synthetic.csv")` to run the code yourself. Its numbers differ somewhat from the ones printed here.]


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(poLCA)
d <- readRDS("../data/liss-health-social-integration/liss_lca_conditions.rds")
items <- c("angina", "heartattack", "hypertension", "cholesterol", "stroke",
           "diabetes", "lung", "asthma", "arthritis", "cancer")
dd <- d[items] + 1                       # poLCA codes categories 1, 2
f  <- as.formula(paste("cbind(", paste(items, collapse = ","), ") ~ 1"))
set.seed(8)
fits <- lapply(1:5, function(k)
  poLCA(f, dd, nclass = k, nrep = if (k == 1) 1 else 10,
        maxiter = 3000, verbose = FALSE))
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(t(sapply(fits, function(m)
  c(classes = length(m$P), loglik = m$llik, npar = m$npar,
    AIC = m$aic, BIC = m$bic))), 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

[2,]       2 -9361.1   21 18764.1 18899.5
[3,]       3 -9286.9   32 18637.7 18843.9
[4,]       4 -9253.5   43 18592.9 18870.0
[5,]       5 -9240.6   54 18589.2 18937.2
```

The `nrep = 10` argument runs the EM algorithm from ten random starting points per model and keeps the best, for the local-maxima reason discussed for K-means; skipping it is the most common error in applied LCA. Each added class costs eleven parameters, one class proportion and ten conditional probabilities, and buys some log-likelihood. The BIC is smallest for the three-class model, while the AIC is still falling at five classes, a disagreement to which @sec-mixture-fit returns. Staying with the BIC's choice, @fig-lca-profile displays the three-class solution as a **profile plot**: one line per class, showing the probability of each diagnosis within that class.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Profile plot of the three-class latent class model of ten physician diagnoses, LISS 2025 (n = 4,647). Lines show the probability of each diagnosis within each class; percentages are the estimated class sizes.](08-unsupervised-clustering-mixtures_files/figure-pdf/fig-lca-profile-1.png){#fig-lca-profile}
:::
:::


The classes are recognizable. The largest, at about three quarters of the sample, is a *healthy* class in which every diagnosis is rare. The second, close to a fifth of respondents, is a *cardiometabolic* class: hypertension in about six of ten members, high cholesterol in more than half, elevated diabetes and arthritis. The smallest, around five percent, is a *respiratory–musculoskeletal* class in which asthma, chronic lung disease, and arthritis are the distinguishing diagnoses. Each respondent additionally receives a posterior probability of belonging to each class, as in the height example, and these posteriors carry real uncertainty: on average the largest posterior is well below 1. That uncertainty must be respected when the classes are used further. Assigning each person to their most likely class and then regressing that assignment on covariates treats the classification as data when it is an estimate, and biases the resulting associations toward zero; the section on external information below describes the corrected procedures for this task.

The local independence assumption can be partly checked. Within each class, pairs of indicators should be unrelated; computing the residual association of each pair within classes, for instance as a chi-square in the class-specific cross-table (a **bivariate residual**), points to pairs the model fails to explain. A large residual between asthma and chronic lung disease, say, would signal that these two diagnoses share something beyond the classes, and a model treating them jointly, or an extra class, may be needed. Such checks cannot validate local independence as a whole, for the reason given in the height example: the classes are latent, so the full pattern of within-class association is not observable.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 8.4"}
(a) In @eq-lca, how many parameters does a $K$-class model for ten binary indicators have, and how many does the saturated model for the $2^{10}$ response patterns have? For which $K$ does the first exceed the second?
(b) State the three restrictions that turn latent profile analysis into K-means.
(c) A colleague fits the three-class model above, assigns every respondent to their most likely class, and reports "class membership predicts mortality". Name the two distinct sources of overconfidence in that sentence.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.4"}
(a) The $K$-class model has $(K - 1) + 10K$ parameters: $K-1$ free class proportions and ten conditional probabilities per class. The saturated model has $2^{10} - 1 = 1023$. The count first exceeds 1023 at $K = 94$ ($11 \times 94 - 1 = 1033$; at $K = 93$ it is 1022), but the model stops being identified far earlier, as @sec-mixture-fit discusses: counting parameters is only the crudest identification check.
(b) Equal-sized spherical covariance matrices in every class (EII), equal class proportions, and hard assignment of each observation to one class (posterior probabilities forced to 0 or 1).
(c) The classification is an estimate with uncertainty, and treating the modal assignment as observed data biases the association toward zero, which the three-step corrections repair. And the classes themselves are model-dependent: as @sec-mixture-fit argues, a well-fitting mixture does not establish that these particular groups exist, so "predicts mortality" inherits every assumption behind the class solution.
:::

## Choosing the number of clusters, and trusting the result {#sec-choosing-k}

Everything above postponed the same decision: how many clusters or classes, and which parameterization. In supervised learning this kind of decision went to the validation set, and the test set evaluated the final choice honestly. Here there is no outcome to score against, so model selection and evaluation take more space in this chapter than in any other. No single tool replaces the missing performance measure; instead a strategy [@hennig2015] assembles five kinds of evidence:

1. **External information**: variables not used to form the clusters, and decisions the clusters are meant to improve.
2. **Visual exploration**: looking at the clusters, in the data's own dimensions or in a two-dimensional map of them.
3. **Stability and sensitivity**: whether the clusters survive changes to the method, the sample, or the features.
4. **Internal validation indices**: numbers computed from the data and the clustering alone, such as the silhouette and the gap statistic.
5. **Tests for clustering structure**: whether there is any evidence of groups at all.

Model-based clustering adds a sixth kind, the fit of the model itself, which the next section treats on its own because it brings back the problem of equivalence. Two of the names need a word, because they resemble the validities of @sec-rq-to-interpretation without being them: an *internal* index scores the partition against the same data that produced it, as the internal validation of @sec-evaluation scored a model on its own data, whereas *external* information is evidence from outside those data about whether the clusters mean what the researcher takes them to mean, which is the concern of construct validity; the causal question of internal validity arises only when the clusters are used for a decision, at the end of the next subsection. The five are taken in turn. None is decisive; a defensible analysis consults several and reports what each said, rather than only the number that agrees with the analyst.

### External information

The strongest evidence for a clustering comes from outside it. If the multimorbidity classes above are real, they should differ in variables that played no part in forming them, in directions that make sense: the cardiometabolic class should be older, and a class defined by asthma and arthritis might be expected to contain more women, since both conditions are more prevalent in women. Such variables are called **criterion** or **distal** variables, and the LISS data carry two:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m3  <- fits[[3]]
ord <- order(m3$P, decreasing = TRUE)      # 1 = largest class
cls <- match(m3$predclass, ord)            # modal class per person
ext <- data.frame(class = cls, age = d$age, female = d$female)
round(t(sapply(split(ext, ext$class), function(s)
  c(n = nrow(s), mean_age = mean(s$age),
    pct_female = 100 * mean(s$female, na.rm = TRUE)))), 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     n mean_age pct_female
1 3782     51.9       52.8
2  723     66.6       51.0
3  142     65.0       59.9
```


:::
:::


The healthy class is fifteen years younger than the other two, and the respiratory–musculoskeletal class is the most female. Neither fact was available to the model, so both count as corroboration. Two refinements turn this from a check into a method. The table assigns each respondent to their modal class, which the previous section warned against: the assignment is an estimate, and treating it as data attenuates the association with any external variable (it also explains why the `n` column gives the healthy class a larger share, and the other two a smaller one, than the estimated proportions of @fig-lca-profile: respondents whose posteriors are uncertain mostly land in the largest class). The **three-step** procedures repair this by estimating the classes first, assigning second, and relating the assignment to external variables third with a correction for the known classification error [@bolck2004; @vermunt2010; @bakk2013]; used this way, three-step analysis is external validation with honest standard errors, and the *size* of the corrected associations is a measure of how much the classes explain. Alternatively the external variable can be let into the model, as a covariate predicting class membership or as a distal outcome predicted by it, and the information criteria of the next section compared with and without the link; a class solution that organizes external variables well then scores better than one that does not, so the criterion then depends partly on external information.

The most demanding external check is to use the clustering for the decision it was built for and to measure whether the decision improves. A market segmentation exists so that different segments can be approached differently; the test of the segmentation is not any index but whether segment-specific campaigns sell more than a single campaign would have [@dolnicar2018]. A multimorbidity typology intended to organize care is validated when care organized by it produces better outcomes than care that ignores it. This reintroduces the supervised setting: as soon as the clustering serves a decision with a measurable consequence, the consequence is an outcome, and everything @sec-evaluation said about honest evaluation applies. It also invokes everything @sec-explanation-prediction said about rain dances, because "does the decision improve" is a causal question that a classification alone cannot answer.

### Visual exploration

In two dimensions the eye is the best cluster validator there is, which is why this chapter chose Old Faithful. In three to ten dimensions, pairwise scatterplots and projections on the directions that best separate the clusters (**discriminant coordinates**) still serve. Beyond that, the current practice is to map the observations into two dimensions with a nonlinear method that tries to keep each observation's neighbours as its neighbours: **t-SNE** [@vandermaaten2008] and **UMAP** [@mcinnes2018] are the popular choices, and their maps have become the standard picture of high-dimensional data in genomics, natural language processing, and increasingly in social science. Old Faithful is a useful test of what such maps do because it needs no mapping: the truth is in @fig-faithful, and @fig-manifold shows what the maps make of it.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Two-dimensional maps of the (standardized) Old Faithful data, coloured by the K-means solution with K = 2. Top left: the data themselves. The other panels are t-SNE with perplexity 5 and 30, and UMAP with 15 neighbours. The two groups survive every map; nothing else does.](08-unsupervised-clustering-mixtures_files/figure-pdf/fig-manifold-1.png){#fig-manifold}
:::
:::


The two groups are preserved in every panel, which is the reason these maps are useful: a clustering found in the full space can be painted onto the map, and clusters that scatter across the map are suspect. Everything else in the picture is produced by the method rather than the data. The elongated, correlated shapes of the real clusters become round blobs or thin strands; the small cluster can be drawn as large as the big one; the distance between the clusters is whatever the algorithm's settings made it; and at low perplexity t-SNE shatters each cluster into a dozen worm-like fragments that a reader without @fig-faithful would count as clusters. These are not errors in the methods: they preserve neighbourhoods, not distances, sizes, or shapes, so a map can show *that* groups exist but not how many, how large, or how far apart [@wattenberg2016]. The hyperparameters (the perplexity, the number of neighbours) and the random seed change the picture, and there is no criterion for choosing them because the map is not fitted to anything. The worst practice, common in fields where these maps are routine, is to run a clustering algorithm on the map coordinates themselves, which clusters the distortions [@chari2023]. The maps are useful for looking at the data, but the clustering should be done on the data themselves.

### Stability and sensitivity

Stability asks whether the clusters would survive a replication. Three kinds of replication can be simulated on the data at hand, corresponding to three things the analyst could have done differently:

- **the method**: a different distance, linkage, parameterization, or $K$;
- **the observations**: a different sample from the same population, imitated by resampling;
- **the features**: a different, equally reasonable, choice of variables.

For each, the question is whether observations land in the same clusters as before, measured by an index of agreement between two partitions that is indifferent to the arbitrary labels: the **Jaccard index** of a cluster is the share of observations in either version of it that are in both, and the **adjusted Rand index (ARI)** [@hubert1985] scores two whole partitions on a scale where 1 is identical and 0 is chance agreement.

*The method.* For Old Faithful with $K = 2$, K-means and hierarchical clustering under every linkage agree almost perfectly (ARI above 0.99). With $K = 3$ the agreement disappears:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
X  <- scale(faithful)                      # standardized, as before
hc <- function(m, k) cutree(hclust(dist(X), method = m), k)
set.seed(1)
parts <- list(kmeans   = kmeans(X, 3, nstart = 25)$cluster,
              complete = hc("complete", 3), average = hc("average", 3),
              single   = hc("single", 3),   ward    = hc("ward.D2", 3))
ari <- outer(names(parts), names(parts), Vectorize(function(a, b)
  adjustedRandIndex(parts[[a]], parts[[b]])))
dimnames(ari) <- list(names(parts), names(parts))
round(ari, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

kmeans     1.00     0.75    0.61   0.59 0.80
complete   0.75     1.00    0.74   0.66 0.74
average    0.61     0.74    1.00   0.85 0.66
single     0.59     0.66    0.85   1.00 0.62
ward       0.80     0.74    0.66   0.62 1.00
```


:::
:::


The five methods produce five different third clusters, one of which (single linkage) is a single outlying eruption. When every reasonable method returns the same partition, the partition is a property of the data; when they disagree, it is a property of the method, and the report should say which method and why.

*The observations.* Bootstrap stability refits the clustering on resamples of the data and records, for each original cluster, the Jaccard agreement with the most similar cluster in each resample [@hennig2007]. The `fpc::clusterboot()` function does this for any clustering method; below, for K-means with two and three clusters:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(fpc)
cb2 <- clusterboot(X, B = 100, clustermethod = kmeansCBI, k = 2,
                   seed = 1, count = FALSE)
cb3 <- clusterboot(X, B = 100, clustermethod = kmeansCBI, k = 3,
                   seed = 1, count = FALSE)
jac <- rbind("K = 2" = c(cb2$bootmean, NA), "K = 3" = cb3$bootmean)
colnames(jac) <- paste("cluster", 1:3)
round(jac, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      cluster 1 cluster 2 cluster 3
K = 2      1.00      0.99        NA
K = 3      0.69      0.91      0.79
```


:::
:::


Both two-cluster solutions recur in essentially every resample. The three-cluster solution is less secure, and Hennig's rule of thumb says how much: a mean Jaccard above 0.85 marks a highly stable cluster, above 0.75 a stable one, between 0.6 and 0.75 a pattern whose exact membership is doubtful, and below 0.6 a cluster not to be trusted. Two of the three clusters pass, and the weakest is one of the two halves into which $K = 3$ cuts the large cluster, a cut the data do not support. This is the bootstrap of @sec-evaluation, estimating sampling variability as before, applied to a partition instead of a coefficient.

*The features.* A clustering is a clustering of whichever variables were included, and a class that depends on one indicator is a class of that indicator. Leaving out each of the ten LISS diagnoses in turn, refitting the three-class model, and comparing the classification with the full model's shows which indicators carry the typology:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ari_drop <- sapply(items, function(drop) {
  keep <- setdiff(items, drop)
  fk   <- as.formula(paste("cbind(", paste(keep, collapse = ","),
                           ") ~ 1"))
  set.seed(8)
  m <- poLCA(fk, dd[keep], nclass = 3, nrep = 10, maxiter = 3000,
             verbose = FALSE)
  adjustedRandIndex(m$predclass, m3$predclass)
})
round(sort(ari_drop), 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
hypertension  cholesterol         lung       asthma     diabetes       cancer 
        0.56         0.62         0.73         0.73         0.80         0.83 
   arthritis  heartattack       angina       stroke 
        0.90         0.97         0.97         0.99 
```


:::

Dropping angina, a heart attack, or a stroke changes almost nothing, because these rare diagnoses contribute little to the class definitions. Dropping hypertension or high cholesterol reshuffles the classes: the cardiometabolic class *is* the co-occurrence of those two, and a study that had not asked about cholesterol would have found a different typology. That is not a flaw in the model, but it is a fact about what the typology means, and it should be reported.

Stability is necessary and not sufficient. A partition along the single dominant variable is stable but uninteresting; conversely, a real but subtle structure can be unstable at the sample size available. Stability rules out one kind of error, mistaking noise for structure, and says nothing about the other kinds.

### Internal validation indices

Internal indices score a clustering from the data and the partition alone. The best known is the **silhouette** [@rousseeuw1987]. For each observation $i$, let $a_i$ be its mean distance to the other members of its own cluster and $b_i$ its mean distance to the members of the nearest other cluster; the silhouette width is

$$
s_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)} ,
$$

which is near 1 for an observation deep inside a compact, well-separated cluster, near 0 for one on the boundary between two clusters, and negative for one that would fit better elsewhere. The **average silhouette width** over all observations summarizes the partition, and the silhouette plot in @fig-silhouette displays each cluster's widths as a sorted bar chart. The **gap statistic** [@tibshirani2001gap] takes a different route: it computes the within-cluster dispersion $W_K$ for each $K$, as K-means does, and compares its logarithm with what the same computation would give on data with no clusters at all, simulated uniformly over the range of the features. The gap is the difference; it is large when the data are much more clustered than featureless data would be, and the recommended choice of $K$ is the smallest $K$ whose gap is within one simulation standard error of the gap at $K + 1$.


::: {.cell}

With K = 3 the large cluster is cut in two, and both halves have low widths: their members are about as close to the other half as to their own.](08-unsupervised-clustering-mixtures_files/figure-pdf/fig-silhouette-1.png){#fig-silhouette}

  mean(silhouette(kmeans(X, k, nstart = 25)$cluster, D)[, "sil_width"]))
gap <- clusGap(X, FUN = function(x, k) kmeans(x, k, nstart = 25),
               K.max = 6, B = 100)

            gap = gap$Tab[, "gap"], SE = gap$Tab[, "SE.sim"]), 3)

Both indices agree with the eye: the silhouette peaks sharply at $K = 2$, and the gap rule stops there as well. Their limitation is that they encode a particular idea of what a cluster is, compact, well separated, roughly round, and take no account of the clustering's aim. Two elongated, touching clusters that a substantive question treats as distinct will score badly on both; a partition that splits one continuous cloud into halves can score well. Different indices formalize different cluster concepts and can rank the same solutions differently, so an index can support a choice made on other grounds but cannot make it.

### Testing for clustering structure

The last kind of evidence asks whether there is any structure to find. The **dip test** [@hartigan1985] tests a single variable, or the pairwise distances, against unimodality, and the Hopkins statistic compares the distances among the observations with the distances to random points in the same space; either can flag data that are simply one diffuse cloud. For mixture models the corresponding tool is the likelihood-ratio test of $K$ against $K+1$ components: twice the difference between the two maximized log-likelihoods, the chi-square difference test of @def-likelihood. The ordinary chi-square theory fails here, because the smaller model sits on the boundary of the larger one, and the accepted replacement is the **bootstrapped likelihood-ratio test**, which simulates the statistic's distribution under the smaller model [@mclachlan1987; @nylund2007]:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(3)
mclustBootstrapLRT(faithful, modelName = "VVV", maxG = 3, nboot = 199,
                   verbose = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Bootstrap sequential LRT for the number of mixture components 
------------------------------------------------------------- 
Model        = VVV 
Replications = 199

1 vs 2   319.065354             0.005
2 vs 3     6.130516             0.580
3 vs 4    31.837839             0.010
```


:::
:::


One component is clearly rejected in favour of two, which answers the structure question: there are clusters. The rest of the table is a warning about sequential testing. Two against three is not rejected, so the procedure stops at two, but three against four would have been, so the "number of components" depends on the order of testing. And with $n$ in the thousands, as in the LISS data, every added class is significant, because the test detects any misfit however small. Tests establish that structure exists, but they are a poor guide to how much.

## Model fit, information criteria, and their limits {#sec-mixture-fit}

For model-based clustering a sixth kind of evidence exists, and it is the one applied work leans on most heavily: the fit of the model. The standard tools are the **AIC** and **BIC**, first met in @sec-anova and defined here,

$$
\text{AIC} = -2\,\ell + 2\,p, \qquad
\text{BIC} = -2\,\ell + p \log n ,
$$

where $\ell$ is the maximized log-likelihood (@def-likelihood), $p$ the number of parameters, and $n$ the sample size; the smaller the better. Each has two justifications, and the one that connects to @sec-evaluation is in terms of overfitting. The in-sample log-likelihood, like the training error of @sec-overfitting, improves with every added class, because the same data that fitted the parameters are scoring them. On average the excess, the *optimism* of the in-sample fit in the sense of @sec-evaluation, amounts to about $2p$ on the $-2\ell$ scale, so the AIC is the in-sample deviance ($-2\ell$) plus an estimate of its optimism: an estimate of $-2$ times the log-likelihood the model would achieve on new data from the same population [@hastie2009, ch. 7]. Comparing AICs is therefore an approximation to comparing models on fresh data, the quantity @sec-evaluation measured by holding data out, and the direct route is also available: the log-likelihood can be cross-validated, scoring each held-out fold under the model fitted to the rest, with all of that chapter's machinery and cautions applying unchanged.

The second justification is the one in the names. Akaike derived the AIC as an estimate of how far the fitted model's distribution lies from the distribution that generated the data, distance being measured by the Kullback–Leibler divergence, an information-theoretic measure of the discrepancy between two distributions. Schwarz derived the BIC as an approximation to the marginal likelihood of the model, the probability of the data averaged over the model's parameters under a prior, which is the quantity a Bayesian analysis (@def-bayes) compares between models; comparing BICs therefore approximates comparing the posterior probabilities of the models.

The BIC's heavier penalty, $p \log n$, gives it a different property. It is consistent: when one of the candidate models is true, the BIC selects it as $n$ grows, whereas the AIC tends to select slightly-too-large models. In mixtures the BIC tends to select fewer, better-separated classes, and it is the default in this literature [@gormley2023]. The vector-quantization trade-off of this chapter's first half is the same computation: the log-likelihood corresponds to the reconstruction error, the penalty to the file size.

The two criteria disagreed on the LISS data, the BIC choosing three classes and the AIC five, and such disagreement is typical rather than exceptional. The AIC aims at predictive accuracy and will add classes that improve the density estimate slightly; the BIC aims at recovering a parsimonious structure. There is no neutral arbiter, because the criteria answer different questions, and the choice between them is a choice about the task. When the classes are to be interpreted and used, parsimony and separation usually matter more than the last increment of fit, which favours the BIC, possibly alongside the **ICL**, a BIC variant that additionally penalizes solutions whose classes overlap so much that observations cannot be confidently assigned [@biernacki2000]. On Old Faithful the difference is visible: the BIC chose three components, the ICL chooses two, because the third component improves fit but reduces certainty of assignment. The next section returns to this.

**Identification, and its empirical failure.** With latent variables, a question that precedes model selection is whether the model is identified at all. The word has been used in three senses so far, each a case of @def-identification: the counting rule of @sec-theory-to-glm, which compares parameters with moments; the equivalent models of @sec-identification, which imply the same observed distribution; and the causal sense of that chapter, whether the design lets the data answer the question. The parametric version needed here asks whether different parameter values of one model could produce the same distribution of the observed data. For mixtures, identification fails by degrees rather than all at once, which makes the failure easy to miss. A latent class model can be formally underidentified, with strictly more parameters than the observed table can support, the parameter count of Exercise 8.4 being only the crudest bound [@goodman1974]. A subtler problem is **empirical underidentification**: the model is identified on paper, but the observed data barely constrain some parameters, so the likelihood surface is nearly flat in some directions. LCA reaches this state quickly, especially with rare indicators, small classes, and generous $K$. The problem has recognizable symptoms. Repeated estimation from many random starts returns different solutions with practically equal log-likelihoods; estimated probabilities land on the boundary at exactly 0 or 1; some class sizes collapse toward zero; and standard errors of some parameters explode. The six-class model for the LISS diagnoses shows all of these symptoms:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sixes <- t(sapply(1:8, function(s) {
  set.seed(100 + s)
  m <- poLCA(f, dd, nclass = 6, nrep = 1, maxiter = 3000, verbose = FALSE)
  c(loglik = m$llik, smallest_class = min(m$P),
    boundary_estimates = sum(unlist(m$probs) < 1e-4 |
                             unlist(m$probs) > 1 - 1e-4))
}))
round(sixes, 2)
```

[4,] -9228.62           0.03                 20
[5,] -9228.63           0.03                 20

Eight starts produce several distinct maxima whose log-likelihoods differ only in the first decimal, each with a dozen or more boundary estimates and smallest classes holding at most a few percent of the sample. None of these solutions can be called "the six-class model": the data cannot tell them apart, and any substantive story told about one of them would have come out differently on the next start. The practical defences follow from the symptoms: always use many random starts and inspect the spread of the maxima, distrust boundary estimates and near-empty classes, and when the syndrome appears, reduce $K$, restrict parameters, or collect more indicators, since each added indicator multiplies the observable information while adding only $K$ parameters.

**Equivalence, one more time.** Even a well-identified, well-fitting mixture supports a weaker conclusion than it appears to, and the reason is not special to mixtures. Every fit statistic in this book, from the chi-square of @sec-theory-to-glm to the BIC above, works the same way: the model implies a distribution for the observed data, and the statistic measures the distance between that implied distribution and the observed one. Two models that imply the same distribution are therefore indistinguishable by any fit statistic, whatever their parameters say, and this is the **equivalence** problem of @sec-theory-to-glm and @sec-identification again. It arises here in two forms. A heavily restricted model with many classes can reproduce the observed distribution as well as a flexible model with few classes; and, as the Old Faithful example showed, a mixture of three components and a mixture of two merged clusters describe one and the same density. Model selection compares only the candidate models the analyst specified, and cannot detect that two candidates are equivalent or that the true model is not among them; this is a general limitation of model selection, supervised or not, that the supervised chapters could ignore only because their candidates were scored on an outcome. Without an outcome, fit cannot distinguish between equivalent descriptions, so the choice among them is made by assumptions, and the inference "the model fits, hence these are the true latent groups" is never available. What is available is the conditional statement used since @sec-identification: *if* the population consists of groups within which the indicators are independent (or normal), *then* the data point to these groups, with this many classes, of these sizes. The assumptions carry the conclusion, and for latent variables some of them are uncheckable in principle, since checking would require observing the variable that is latent.

An uncheckable assumption can still be supported, by design. Local independence is an assumption about *why the indicators are correlated*: it says the latent class is the only common cause, so that within a class the remaining variation in each indicator is noise specific to that indicator. Whether that is plausible depends on where the indicators come from. Ten self-reported diagnoses from a single questionnaire share a respondent, a sitting, a memory, and a reporting style, and any of these can correlate the indicators within classes, violating local independence in ways no fit statistic will reliably flag. Now consider instead a design in which one indicator of, say, problematic debt comes from a survey question, a second from an administrative register of payment arrears, and a third from a digital trace of account activity. These three measurements share essentially one thing: the person's true state. Their error sources, self-presentation, administrative lag, algorithmic misclassification, are distinct by construction, so conditional independence given the latent state is a designed property rather than a hope. The same assumption that is implausible within a single survey becomes credible across sources; the model is unchanged, only the design behind its inputs differs. Latent variable models do not remove the need to think about inputs; they move it from the interpretation of coefficients to the provenance of indicators.

## Merging components into clusters {#sec-merging}

The mismatch between components and clusters, which has come up three times in this chapter, has a solution of its own. The mixture model's building blocks are normal components (or, in LCA, locally independent classes), and the information criteria count *components*: the BIC picks the number of normal densities needed to describe the data's density well. A cluster in the researcher's sense is something else, a group of observations that belong together, and a group that is not normally shaped needs several components to trace it. On Old Faithful the BIC needed three components for two clusters. On a dataset of 200 crabs of two species and two sexes, four groups by construction, the BIC selects *nine* components, and @hennig2010 shows that they describe the density better than four would; the count is not wrong, it is answering a different question. Practice in the social and health sciences almost always equates classes with components, and so it is caught between two errors: accept the criterion's count and report subgroups that are shape artefacts, or override it by hand and lose the fit.

**Merging** resolves the dilemma, and it is underused outside statistics. The idea is to separate the two questions. First fit the mixture with as many components as the BIC selects, so that the density is described well. Then combine components hierarchically into clusters: start with every component as its own cluster, find the pair of clusters whose union is most cluster-like, merge them, and repeat until a stopping rule says the remaining clusters are distinct [@hennig2010]. Everything depends on the criterion for "most cluster-like", and several exist. The **entropy** criterion of @baudry2010, implemented in `mclust::clustCombi()`, uses the entropy of the classification, $-\sum_i \sum_k z_{ik} \log z_{ik}$, where $z_{ik}$ is observation $i$'s posterior probability for cluster $k$: it is zero when every posterior is 0 or 1 and grows with the uncertainty of assignment. The criterion merges the pair whose union most reduces this entropy, so that the resulting clusters are ones observations can be assigned to confidently; the decrease in entropy as clusters are merged shows a clear elbow at the right number of clusters. **Unimodality** criteria merge two components when their union has a single mode, checked along the ridgeline connecting the two component means or by the dip test, and stop when a merge would produce a bimodal cluster. **Misclassification** criteria, such as the Bhattacharyya distance between the components or a direct estimate of how many observations one component would misassign to the other, merge components so overlapping that they cannot be told apart, and stop when the remaining clusters can. @fig-merge shows the entropy version on Old Faithful, starting from the three components of @fig-mclust.

The entropy of the three-component classification is about 42 nats (a *nat* is the unit of entropy when natural logarithms are used, as in the formula above), nearly all of it from eruptions whose assignment between the two overlapping components in the upper right is uncertain; merging those two removes almost all of it, leaving half a nat, and merging the two remaining clusters would remove only that half, because they were already separated. The elbow is at two clusters. The merged solution agrees with K-means almost perfectly (ARI 0.98) while keeping everything the mixture model offered, the posterior probabilities, the estimated proportions, and a density that fits. The alternative repair, selecting by the ICL instead of the BIC, reaches two components directly on these data, but it does so by accepting a worse density in exchange for separation, which matters whenever the model is also used to describe or generate data; merging keeps the fit and adds the clusters on top. The same logic applies to latent class analysis: fit the classes the BIC asks for, then merge classes between which the posterior probabilities cannot discriminate, and report the merged clusters as the typology while the full solution stays on record as the model.

The choice of merging criterion cannot be made by the data, because, as @hennig2010 states, the merging problem is not identified. A mixture of two normal components is the same density whether the components are called one cluster or two, so whether they should be merged is not a question about the data but about the **cluster concept**, what the researcher means by a cluster. If clusters are modes, two components whose union is unimodal are one cluster. If clusters are dense patterns that stand out from a diffuse background, a narrow component sitting inside a wide one is a cluster of its own, though the union is unimodal. If clusters are groups that can be assigned to reliably, the criterion is misclassification. These concepts give different answers on the same data, and no fit statistic can adjudicate, because fit is identical across them. This is not a defect of merging but a general fact about clustering that merging makes explicit. The number of clusters depends on the data together with an idea of what a cluster is, and the idea should come from the task. A multimorbidity typology meant to guide treatment wants classes that can be assigned reliably; a typology meant to describe distinct disease processes wants modes. Which concept applies should be stated at the start of the analysis.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 8.6"}
(a) Rank the five kinds of evidence of @sec-choosing-k by how much each depends on the analyst's cluster concept, and justify the two ends of your ranking.
(b) A t-SNE map of a 40-item questionnaire shows six clear islands. List three questions to ask before believing there are six types of respondent.
(c) On the LISS data, dropping hypertension changed the three-class solution substantially (ARI 0.56). A colleague concludes the typology is "unreliable". Give a more precise reading.
(d) Explain why a 4-component mixture merged into 2 clusters and a 2-component mixture fitted directly can have identical clusters and different log-likelihoods, and when the difference matters.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.6"}
(a) Internal indices depend most, because each index *is* a formalized cluster concept (compact and separated, for the silhouette). Tests for clustering structure depend least, since they ask only whether the data depart from one homogeneous cloud, though the choice of null hypothesis is itself a weak concept. External validation sits in between: it depends on the concept only through the choice of external variables and decisions.
(b) Whether the islands survive a different perplexity and seed; whether a clustering fitted in the 40-dimensional data, painted on the map, respects the islands; and whether the islands are response *patterns* rather than persons, since 40 categorical items generate many identical rows that the map draws as tight clumps.
(c) The typology is reliable *given its indicators*: resampling respondents leaves it intact. What the feature check shows is that the cardiometabolic class is largely defined by hypertension and cholesterol, so the typology is a typology of this item set, and a study with different items would find a different one. That is a statement about meaning and generalization, not about noise.
(d) The four-component model describes the density with more flexibility, so its log-likelihood is at least as high; merging changes the labels, not the density. The difference matters when the model's density is used, for posterior probabilities near the boundaries, for simulating data, or for prediction, and does not matter when only the hard partition is used.
:::

## Evaluation without an outcome

This chapter closes the machine learning part of the book, and its conclusion runs opposite to that of the two chapters before it. Chapters 6 and 7 built their case on output validity: fix the task and the metric, and models can be compared empirically, with assumptions demoted to whatever helps prediction. That case rested entirely on the existence of a supervisor, an observed outcome against which performance could be measured honestly. Unsupervised learning has no such outcome, and the consequences run through this chapter. The number of clusters is not measurable but chosen, with criteria that answer different questions; the clusters themselves are conditional on assumptions, some uncheckable in principle; equivalent models tell different stories about the same fit; the definition of a cluster comes from the task, not the data; and the strongest support available comes not from any statistic but from design, in the provenance of the indicators and in validation against external information. Without a supervisor, input validity returns as the central concern. The questions of chapters 1 to 4, what was measured, how, on whom, and what must be assumed, are not alternatives to machine learning; machine learning depends on them whenever honest output measurement is unavailable. A researcher needs both approaches, and needs to know which one a given problem calls for.

## What to carry forward {.unnumbered}

No chapter follows this one, so its results stand on their own: a clustering algorithm groups observations by a distance, so the choice of distance, of standardization and of linkage decides what is found, K-means must be run from many starts, and neither method decides how many clusters there are ("Clustering by distance"). A mixture model turns the same task into a statistical model with an unobserved discrete variable, its parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm, and its output for each observation is a posterior probability of class membership by Bayes' rule, @eq-bayes-mixture, rather than a hard label; K-means is the special case with equal spherical components and hard assignment, and the model's within-class assumption, normality or local independence, is what identifies it and what the data cannot check ("Clustering with a model: mixtures"). Without an outcome, the number of clusters is chosen rather than measured, and the choice is supported by five kinds of evidence, of which external information and stability are the strongest and internal indices and tests the weakest ("Choosing the number of clusters, and trusting the result"). The AIC estimates the fit a model would achieve on new data and the BIC approximates the evidence for the model, so they answer different questions and often disagree, and both can be defeated by empirical underidentification and by equivalent models, which fit statistics cannot separate ("Model fit, information criteria, and their limits"). Components are not clusters: a criterion counts the densities needed to describe the data, and turning them into clusters requires a cluster concept that the task, not the data, supplies ("Merging components into clusters"). When no outcome is available, the input questions of chapters 1 to 4, what was measured, how, and on whom, become the main support for the result ("Evaluation without an outcome").
