## Further study {.unnumbered}

Clustering and mixture modelling extend in many directions, and this chapter has covered only the core. The main extensions, and where to read about them, are the following. Covariates can be built into the mixture, so that class membership depends on background variables (**latent class regression**, or mixtures of experts), and the classes can predict distal outcomes; @vermunt2010 and @bakk2013 cover the estimation issues, and `poLCA` fits the regression version. Repeated measurements bring **latent transition analysis**, in which people move between classes over time, and **growth mixture** or group-based trajectory models, in which the classes are shapes of development [@collins2010; @nagin2005]. Mixed continuous and categorical indicators, counts, rankings, sequences of states, curves from sensors, and networks each have their own mixture models, surveyed in @gormley2023 and @bouveyron2019. On the algorithmic side, density-based methods such as DBSCAN find clusters of arbitrary shape without a $K$ [@ester1996], and in high dimensions the question of *which* variables to cluster on becomes a model selection problem of its own. For texts, images, and other unstructured data the current practice is to cluster embeddings produced by a neural network, which raises every question of this chapter with the added difficulty that the features are themselves learned. Chapter 12 of @james2021 covers clustering from the machine learning side; @oberski2016 is a compact introduction to latent profile and latent class analysis from the social science side, on which this chapter's treatment of mixtures draws; @hennig2015 is the guide to choosing a clustering strategy that this chapter's evaluation section follows; and @mclachlan2000 is the comprehensive reference on finite mixture models.

## Test yourself {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 8.A"}
A municipal health service wants to identify types of problematic alcohol use among 12,000 residents, combining three indicators: a survey self-report, emergency-department records, and pharmacy dispensing data.

(a) Say why this three-source design supports the local independence assumption better than three survey questions would, and name one residual threat to it.
(b) Specify a defensible procedure for choosing the number of classes, naming at least three distinct tools and the order in which you would consult them.
(c) The four-class solution includes a class of 1.5 percent of residents with two conditional probabilities estimated at exactly zero. What do you suspect, and what three checks would you run?
(d) The service wants to target an intervention at the highest-risk class. Which chapters' machinery does that decision invoke beyond this one's, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.A"}
(a) The three sources share the resident's true state but little else: survey errors come from self-presentation and recall, ED records from presentation and coding practices, dispensing data from prescription behaviour. Distinct error mechanisms make within-class independence a designed property rather than an assumption of convenience. A residual threat: all three sources may miss the same people, for example residents who avoid care entirely, which correlates the indicators within the healthy class.
(b) Fit $K = 1, 2, \ldots$ with many random starts; consult the BIC (and ICL) for a defensible range; run the bootstrapped likelihood-ratio test on the boundary candidates; check stability by refitting on bootstrap resamples; and weigh interpretability and class separation for the final choice, documenting the whole path rather than the winner alone.
(c) Empirical underidentification. Check the spread of log-likelihoods across many starts; inspect standard errors around the boundary estimates; and refit with $K - 1$ classes and with the boundary parameters restricted, comparing fit.
(d) Targeting is an intervention, so its justification is causal: the designs of @sec-rq-to-interpretation and the identification reasoning of @sec-identification. That the class predicts harm is an umbrella claim; that intervening on its members reduces harm is a rain-dance claim, in the vocabulary of @sec-explanation-prediction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 8.B"}
Two published analyses of the same national survey report latent class models of adolescent risk behaviour. Study 1 reports a four-class model with unrestricted conditional probabilities. Study 2 reports a seven-class model in which many conditional probabilities are constrained equal across classes. Both report excellent and nearly identical fit, and each claims to have found "the" typology.

(a) Explain why the near-identical fit is not surprising, using this chapter's vocabulary and its antecedents in earlier chapters.
(b) Neither study used multiple random starts. What specifically is at risk in each?
(c) A reader asks which typology is true. Write the two-sentence honest answer.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.B"}
(a) The two models are close to equivalent: restrictions traded against classes can leave the implied distribution of the observed responses nearly unchanged, so fit cannot separate them, just as equivalent path models fit identically in @sec-identification. The data constrain the observed distribution; the partition of that distribution into classes comes from the assumptions.
(b) Each reported solution may be a local maximum, so the published parameters, and with them the substantive typology, might not even be the best solution of the authors' own model; and with seven classes, Study 2 is additionally at high risk of empirical underidentification, with several near-equal maxima describing different typologies.
(c) Neither is known to be true: each is the best description of the data conditional on its own restrictions, and the data cannot adjudicate between the restrictions. What can be reported honestly is the conditional claim, together with checks, stability, external validation, design of the indicators, that make one set of assumptions more defensible than the other.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 8.C"}
Return to the Old Faithful data.

(a) Fit `Mclust(faithful, G = 2, modelNames = "VVV")` and report the posterior probabilities of the eruption in row 244 of `faithful`, which lasted 2.9 minutes after a 63-minute wait. Then run `kmeans(scale(faithful), 2, nstart = 25)` and say what it reports for the same eruption. Which of the two outputs would you show a park ranger, and why?
(b) mclust's chosen model used three components for two clusters. Explain to a non-statistician colleague why "the algorithm found three groups" would be a misreading.
(c) Suppose eruptions were recorded by two different instruments, and the instrument identity were unavailable. What syndrome from this chapter should the analyst worry about, and which checks apply?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.C"}
(a) The mixture gives this eruption a posterior of 0.80 for the short-eruption component and 0.20 for the long one (in this fit mclust numbers the short component 2, but the labels are arbitrary), and it is the only eruption in the data whose largest posterior is below 0.98. K-means reports one cluster label, the short cluster, and nothing else: the label is the same for this eruption as for one in the middle of the cluster. Show the ranger the posterior. A one-in-five chance of a long eruption is information a hard label hides, and the mixture also estimates the proportions of the two types, 0.64 long and 0.36 short, with standard errors; K-means's hard assignments assert certainty the data do not contain.
(b) The three normal components are the model's building blocks for describing the shape of the data's density, not necessarily the groups of interest: one banana-shaped cluster needs two ellipses to trace it. The components describe the density; the clusters are the substantive claim.
(c) An unmeasured grouping variable, the instrument, can generate spurious classes or distort real ones, and within-"type" correlation induced by the instrument violates local independence. Stability checks across subsamples, external validation against any available metadata, and scrutiny of whether extra small classes appear with boundary estimates are the applicable defences.
:::

This exercise is optional and more challenging than the others: it connects the posterior probabilities of this chapter to the logistic regression of @sec-theory-to-glm, and nothing else depends on it.

Take the two-component height mixture of @eq-mixture with a common standard deviation $\sigma$ in both groups. Show that the posterior log-odds of being a man, $\log[\Pr(X = 1 \mid h)/\Pr(X = 2 \mid h)]$, is linear in $h$, with slope $(\mu_1 - \mu_2)/\sigma^2$ and intercept $\log(\pi_1^X/\pi_2^X) - (\mu_1^2 - \mu_2^2)/(2\sigma^2)$.

(a) Conclude that classifying by the posterior is a logistic regression of the (unobserved) class on height, with known coefficients.
(b) Solve for the height at which the posterior is 0.5 and evaluate it with $\mu_1 = 1.77$, $\mu_2 = 1.62$, $\sigma = 0.07$ and $\pi_1^X = \pi_2^X$.
(c) What does this say about the relation between the mixture model of this chapter and the logistic regression of @sec-theory-to-glm?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 8.D"}
Write @eq-bayes-mixture for each group and divide the two: the denominators $p(h)$ cancel, leaving $\log(\pi_1^X/\pi_2^X) + \log \text{Normal}(h; \mu_1, \sigma) - \log \text{Normal}(h; \mu_2, \sigma)$. Each log-density is $-(h - \mu_k)^2/(2\sigma^2)$ plus a constant that is the same for both groups because $\sigma$ is common. Expanding the squares, the $h^2$ terms cancel, and what remains is $\log(\pi_1^X/\pi_2^X) - (\mu_1^2 - \mu_2^2)/(2\sigma^2) + h\,(\mu_1 - \mu_2)/\sigma^2$.
(a) The log-odds of class membership is an intercept plus a slope times height: the logistic model of @sec-theory-to-glm with the class as the outcome, except that the coefficients are functions of the mixture parameters instead of numbers estimated from labelled data. With the values in (b) the slope is 30.6 per metre and the intercept $-51.9$.
(b) Setting the log-odds to zero gives $h = (\mu_1 + \mu_2)/2 + \sigma^2 \log(\pi_2^X/\pi_1^X)/(\mu_1 - \mu_2)$. With equal proportions the second term vanishes and the boundary is the midpoint, 1.695 m; the chapter's unequal standard deviations move it to 1.694 m, as Exercise 8.3(b) found. With men at 30 percent the second term is $0.07^2 \log(0.7/0.3)/0.15 = 0.028$ and the boundary moves to 1.723 m, which is why Exercise 8.3(c) found a posterior near 0.5 at 1.72 m.
(c) Supervised logistic regression estimates these coefficients from data in which the class is observed. The mixture arrives at the same decision boundary from data in which the class is never observed, by assuming the shape of the distribution within each class. The assumption replaces the labels, which is this chapter's argument in one formula.
:::
